items.title: Linux Kernel Gets AI-Assisted Code
points: Linus Torvalds submitted Linux kernel changes written with Claude Code, stating the code, tests, and review were all created "with an LLM coding assistant under my direction."
The fix addresses contention when many tasks read small pieces of the same file simultaneously (a performance bottleneck compared to cars backing up at a single toll booth).
Speed tests on Torvalds's machine showed significant improvement, though the changes haven't been merged into Linux yet.
Torvalds directed the work and reviewed results himself, underscoring that human validation of AI output remains critical in high-stakes software.

items.title: AI Reads Multiple Years of Mammograms at Once
points: NYU researchers trained a system on 3D mammograms (scans capturing breast tissue in thin layers rather than flat images) from over 161,000 women to estimate five-year breast cancer risk by tracking tissue changes year-to-year.
It outperformed standard screening methods relying on family history and breast density; density surprisingly didn't correlate with risk as expected.
Benefit: personalized screening with extra tests for high-risk women and fewer for low-risk ones, using scans patients already had.
Currently a research tool tested at one health system on one scanner brand; further testing at other hospitals is planned before clinical use.

items.title: Meta's Muse Wonder Handles Multi-Step Tasks Across Apps
points: Meta launched Muse Wonder, an AI agent demonstrated creating a wedding seating chart from "who-can't-sit-together" rules and building a running plan by jumping between browser and other apps.
It remembers information across conversations and tries alternative approaches when stuck rather than asking for help, checking with the user before important actions.
Currently available to developers; launching soon in Meta's Muse app for subscribers.
It's a late-stage entrant to task-handling AI; the real test is whether it feels different from ChatGPT or Gemini already in use.

items.title: Humanoids Enter Grocery Store Night Shifts
points: A Danish supermarket chain signed a multi-year deal with HIVE Robots to test humanoid robots restocking shelves overnight, using two robot heights (4'7" and 5'11") to reach all shelf levels.
Remote-trained pilots can take control from anywhere when robots get stuck, enabling real-store deployment before full autonomy exists.
The chain aims for three to five robots per store working around the clock, positioned as backup for staff rather than replacements.
Remote pilot availability is the key enabler, allowing gradual autonomous capability build-out while robots operate in production stores today.

items.title: Structuring Your Champion Network: The Four Stages
points: Stage 1: Define the goal\u2014clarify who builds, what's expected from others, how AI spreads from the field, and how champions interface with central teams, then document it with IT and security agreement.
Stage 2: Nominate peers who are already sophisticated AI users, sought out by teammates for guidance, and have manager support, avoiding senior self-nominees, the busiest person, or new hires.
Stage 3: Train on real work; readiness means each champion delivers one production use case from their own team by the end of training.
Stage 4: Ensure continuation through dual sponsors (one from HR/L&D, one from AI), brief champions' managers, and keep the program a living entity with continuous recruitment.

items.title: The Champion's End-to-End Workflow
points: Use case identification: be conservative about cost and value, and check whether the solution already exists elsewhere before proceeding.
Solution selection: weigh reuse, buy, build, or backlog before defaulting to building, picking the simplest option (shared chat, skill, automation, then agent).
Pre-build definition: document who it's for, what knowledge it needs, how users interact with it, what it must never do, who validates output, and how success is measured.
Deployment and evaluation is where most projects fail\u2014the solution must survive past day one and be trustworthy enough for user hands.

items.title: Champion Profiles and Their Differences
points: Ambassadors drive adoption through use case showcases, peer training, and tooling feedback but don't build production systems.
Ambassador builders build for themselves and their immediate team within defined scope, acting like product managers beyond that boundary.

Internal forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) are professional builders embedded in business teams, often subject matter experts who pivoted into technical delivery, taking ideas to production end-to-end.

items.title: The High-Stakes Shift: Agentic Coding and Non-Technical Builders
points: Non-technical employees using agentic coding tools (autonomous AI systems that write and execute code without human intervention at each step) are now solving parts of their jobs, creating both capability gains and security risks.
Agents can escape intended boundaries and integrate with other systems unexpectedly, making governance harder than with traditional code.

The recommended response is enablement and infrastructure\u2014training more subject matter experts and investing in guardrails\u2014rather than prohibition, treating these builders as mission-critical.

issues.subject: How to Go from AI Power User to AI Leader

headlines: AI power users embedded in business teams—called champions—are the highest-ROI lever for enterprise AI adoption when organized into structured internal networks.
Champions operate as 'peer plus one' within their teams, showing real use cases and moving peers forward without formal authority, spanning roles from ambassadors to internal deployed engineers.
Success depends entirely on what happens after certification: strong programs need dual sponsors (HR/L&D and AI), manager alignment, and continuous nomination of new members.
Champions must master the full pipeline from use case identification through deployment and evaluation, not just tool skills, to avoid building solutions that don't survive contact with users.
Agentic coding tools (AI systems that can write and execute code autonomously) are creating non-technical builders who need security guardrails and infrastructure support as they scale.

points: Stage 1: Define the goal by clarifying who builds, what's expected from others, how AI spreads from the field, and how champions interface with central teams—then write it down with IT and security agreement.

Stage 2: Nominate peers who are already sophisticated AI users, are sought out by teammates for guidance, and have manager support for the work—avoid senior self-nominees, the busiest person, or new hires.
Stage 3: Train on real work; readiness means each champion delivers one production use case from their own team by the end of training.

Stage 4: Ensure continuation through dual sponsors (one from HR/L&D, one from AI), brief champions' managers to close expectations gaps, and keep the program as a living entity with graceful exits and continuous recruitment.

Pre-build definition: document who it's for, what knowledge it needs, how users interact with it, what it must never do, who validates output, and how success is measured.
Deployment and evaluation: ensure the solution survives past day one and establish whether the output is trustworthy enough for user hands; this is where most projects fail.

Ambassador builders: build for themselves and their immediate team within defined scope, act like product managers beyond that boundary.
Internal forward-deployed engineers (FDEs): professional builders embedded in business teams, often subject matter experts who pivoted into technical delivery; take ideas to production end-to-end.
